lead.intro: Every protocol this service speaks, every endpoint it registers and every specification it implements. The endpoint list is read from the running Express router on each request, not from a list kept by hand, so it cannot claim an endpoint that is not there or miss one that is. Issuer identifier {issuer}; the realm's issuer, in every protocol, {wsTrustIssuer}.
lead.unstamped: — computed at startup rather than stamped into a build, so this process is a checkout rather than an artifact
lead.rfc9700: , which RFC 9700 mode turns on — section 2.1 says an authorization response must not be sent over an unencrypted connection
lead.httpsRest: ), with the same certificate LDAPS 636 serves, issued under this service's own Root. It is regenerated on every start unless tls.certificateFile supplies one, so fetch it from /tls/server-certificate and trust it — without verification the first time, since there is no plain port left to fetch it from.

protocols.heading: Protocols this service speaks
protocols.lead: Thirteen families. The count on each card is how many rows that family has in the tables below, and it is not a measure of how much of the protocol is here: four of these live mostly on a raw socket and two register no route at all, and this page is built by walking the Express router. Where that is the case the card says where the protocol really is.
testDouble: This is a test double. It signs everything with a key generated fresh at each start, it never checks a password, and it does not validate access tokens issued by a separate authorization server. The coverage column below says where each specification is implemented in full and where the shape is right but the enforcement is deliberately absent.
as.heading: Authorization servers
as.lead: This process publishes {n} authorization servers, and only the endpoint PATTERN is on the list below — the walk that builds this page sees /:as/oauth2/… as one route however many names have been served through it. Each has its own metadata, its own capabilities and its own issuer, and what its document advertises is what its endpoints do. A name that has never been asked for is not here: a name becomes an authorization server BY being asked for, with the same capabilities the default one has, so the set of possible ones is every string and the set of real ones is this.
as.configureRest: — what a profile publishes is what that authorization server enforces, so narrowing code_challenge_methods_supported there refuses the other method at that server's own authorization endpoint and nowhere else.
inStep: Every registered route is described, every description matches a registered route ({rows} endpoints), and every one of the {protocols} protocol families above names a group that is here and a specification that exists.

specs.heading: Specifications implemented
machineReadable: Machine-readable: {base}/admin/sts-metadata?format=json, which is what the button at the top hands you as a file. It is behind the console gate like the page, so a program fetching it signs in at /authn/login first, or reads the same service through /admin-api, which is not gated. This document is not a specification-defined discovery document — for those, see /.well-known/openid-configuration, /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server, /.well-known/openid-credential-issuer, /.well-known/jwt-vc-issuer, /.well-known/did.json and /.well-known/did-configuration.json.
